title: Twin Rivers Paper Co. LLC v. SEC (2019)
shortTitle: Twin Rivers Paper Co. LLC v. SEC — zone-of-interests note
summary: Paper companies whose only stake in an SEC disclosure rule is lost demand for paper are outside the zone of interests of the securities laws, and an organization that fails to identify injured members with its opening brief lacks standing.
notes:
Key line: "Because the securities laws impose no meaningful constraint on the Industry Petitioners' ability and incentive to push paper regardless of the interests or preferences of shareholders, the controlling precedent here is HWTC." Judge Katsas, for the court.

Citation: 934 F.3d 607 (D.C. Cir. 2019).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were Twin Rivers Paper Company LLC and three paper industry organizations, referred to as the Industry Petitioners, together with Consumer Action, a nonprofit membership organization representing consumer interests. Respondent was the Securities and Exchange Commission, which adopted the rule under review. Amici supporting the petitioners included companies, nonprofits and a labor union; amici supporting the SEC included the Investment Company Institute. The paper industry wanted to preserve the demand for printed shareholder reports. Consumer Action claimed to speak for investors who prefer paper.
sections.Material Facts: The SEC requires investment companies such as mutual funds to send periodic shareholder reports to investors. Before 2018 the default was paper delivery unless an investor chose electronic delivery. In June 2018 the Commission adopted Rule 30e-3, 83 Fed. Reg. 29158, allowing funds to post reports online and mail paper copies only on request. The SEC projected savings of about $140 million a year, which would ordinarily pass to investors because printing costs are paid from fund assets, and found that many investors prefer online access. The rule required funds to keep mailing paper reports until at least January 1, 2021, to send a paper notice with a toll-free number for each report posted online, and to mail a requested paper copy within three business days at no cost. The Industry Petitioners alleged that the rule would reduce demand for paper. Consumer Action's affidavit referred to unnamed members, followers and supporters who prefer paper.
sections.Procedural History: The petitioners sought review of the rule directly in the D.C. Circuit under the judicial review provisions of the Securities Act, the Exchange Act and the Investment Company Act. Consumer Action submitted only a general organizational affidavit with its opening brief and supplied individual member affidavits for the first time with its reply brief. The court heard argument on March 12, 2019, and on August 16, 2019 denied the petition for review.
sections.Issue: A petitioner seeking direct review of agency action in the D.C. Circuit must establish Article III standing with evidence submitted no later than its opening brief, and a party invoking a statutory review provision must also assert interests within the zone of interests the statute protects or regulates. Consumer Action relied on unnamed members, and the paper industry relied on lost sales of paper. Does Consumer Action have Article III standing on behalf of its members, and do the paper industry petitioners fall within the zone of interests of the securities laws, so that either may obtain review of Rule 30e-3?
sections.Holding: No on both questions. Consumer Action failed to establish standing because it did not identify injured members by affidavit with its opening brief as Sierra Club v. EPA and Circuit Rule 28(a)(7) require, and its late reply-brief affidavits did not qualify for the good-cause exception. The Industry Petitioners' interest in selling paper does not coincide systemically with the interests of investors, so they are outside the zone of interests of the securities laws. The petition was denied.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Katsas first applied the circuit's rules for proving standing on direct review of agency action. An organization suing for its members must show that at least one identified member suffered a concrete injury, ordinarily through individual affidavits filed with the opening brief. Consumer Action's affidavit named no members, described its membership vaguely, and referred only to a general preference for paper and unspecified burdens, which was not proof of a direct, real and palpable injury. The court refused to excuse the forfeiture because the organization could not reasonably have believed its barebones affidavit sufficed or that its standing was self-evident from the rulemaking record, and it distinguished Communities Against Runway Expansion, where the opening brief affidavits had already established the members' identity and location. Turning to the Industry Petitioners, the court explained that the zone-of-interests test admits intended beneficiaries and other suitable challengers whose interests coincide systemically rather than fortuitously with those of beneficiaries. Under Hazardous Waste Treatment Council v. Thomas, a party with a commercial stake in a regulatory choice is not a suitable challenger unless the statute channels its incentives into enforcing a defined boundary. The securities laws direct the SEC to consider the public interest, investor protection and efficiency, but impose no constraint that aligns paper companies with shareholders, so the paper industry's interest was too remote.
